title: Topic Sentences and Main Ideas
objectives: Keep paragraphs focused on one idea
target_phrases: A better topic sentence would be...

dialogue.title: ESL Writing Class
dialogue.context: Ahmed's writing teacher explains how to write strong topic sentences and identify main ideas in paragraphs.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: Today we're learning about topic sentences. Who can tell me what a topic sentence is?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Is it the first sentence in a paragraph?

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: Often, yes! But more importantly, it's the sentence that states the main idea of the paragraph. Everything else in the paragraph should support it.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: So if my paragraph is about why I like Portland, the topic sentence should say that?

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: Exactly! For example: 'Portland is a great city for many reasons.' Then your supporting details explain those reasons.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: What if I write about Portland's weather, and then food, and then people? Is that okay?

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: That's three different topics! Pick one for each paragraph. If your topic sentence is 'Portland has wonderful food,' then every sentence should be about food.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.text: What happens if I go off-topic?

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: Your paragraph loses focus. Look at this example: 'Portland has great food. There are many food carts. I also like the weather. The restaurants are diverse.' See the problem?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Oh! The sentence about weather doesn't belong. It's off-topic.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: Perfect! That sentence breaks the unity of the paragraph. Remove it or save it for a different paragraph about weather.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: So one paragraph, one main idea?

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.text: Exactly. Your topic sentence announces the main idea, and every other sentence supports it with details, examples, or explanations.

examples: Learning English is challenging but rewarding.
Public transportation in Portland is convenient and affordable.
Healthy eating requires planning and discipline.
My first job taught me valuable lessons.
Regular exercise provides many health benefits.

pattern_drills.pattern: The main idea of this paragraph is [summary]
examples: The main idea is that exercise improves health.
The main idea is why Ahmed moved to America.
The main idea is the benefits of learning languages.
The main idea is how to save money effectively.
The main idea is Portland's diverse food scene.
Portland has excellent public transit. The MAX light rail connects the city. Buses run frequently. Fares are affordable.
Learning English takes dedication. I study every day. I practice with native speakers. I watch English TV shows.
Exercise improves health in many ways. It strengthens muscles. It reduces stress. It boosts energy.

listening_exercises.transcript: A strong topic sentence has two parts: the topic (what you're writing about) and the controlling idea (your specific point about the topic). Example: 'Learning English is challenging.' Topic = learning English. Controlling idea = challenging. All supporting sentences should explain why or how it's challenging. If you start talking about something else, you've lost focus.
listening_exercises.question: What two parts does a topic sentence need?

listening_exercises.transcript: Topic sentences are usually at the beginning of paragraphs, but not always. Some writers put them at the end for emphasis, or occasionally in the middle. However, for ESL writers learning paragraph structure, it's best to start with the topic sentence first. This clearly announces your main idea and helps you stay focused while writing.
listening_exercises.question: Where do most paragraphs place the topic sentence?

listening_exercises.transcript: Unity means every sentence in a paragraph relates to the topic sentence. If a sentence doesn't support the main idea, it's off-topic and should be removed. Test each sentence by asking: 'Does this directly support my topic sentence?' If the answer is no, delete it or save it for another paragraph. This keeps your writing focused and clear.
listening_exercises.question: What is unity in a paragraph?
options: Every sentence supports the topic sentence
Starting every sentence the same way

speaking_tasks.prompt: Create a topic sentence about something you're good at. Then give 3 supporting details. Record for 25 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: Here's my topic sentence: 'I am good at learning new languages.' Now my three supporting details: First, I learn vocabulary quickly by reading and using flashcards. Second, I'm not afraid to make mistakes when speaking, which helps me improve faster. Third, I practice every day by watching shows and talking with native speakers. All three details support my topic sentence about being good at languages.

speaking_tasks.prompt: Listen to this paragraph and identify which sentence is off-topic: 'Portland has great food. There are many food carts downtown. I also enjoy hiking. The restaurants serve cuisine from around the world.' Record your answer.
speaking_tasks.example: The sentence that's off-topic is 'I also enjoy hiking.' The paragraph's main idea is about Portland's food, but hiking is not related to food. The other sentences all support the idea that Portland has great food - they mention food carts, restaurants, and diverse cuisine. The hiking sentence should be removed or saved for a different paragraph about outdoor activities in Portland.

writing_tasks.prompt: Write a topic sentence about why you moved to a new place or started learning English. Then write 3-4 supporting sentences. (60-80 words)
writing_tasks.example: Topic sentence: I moved to America for better opportunities for my family. Supporting details: First, the education system here is excellent, and I want my children to have access to good schools. Second, there are more job opportunities in my field than in my home country. Third, America offers political stability and safety, which is important for raising children. Finally, I can earn enough money to support my extended family back home. Each of these sentences directly supports my topic sentence about why I moved.

writing_tasks.prompt: Read this paragraph and identify the topic sentence and one off-topic sentence: 'Exercise is essential for good health. It strengthens your heart and lungs. I also like watching movies. Regular physical activity helps you maintain a healthy weight. Exercise reduces stress and improves mood.' (40-50 words explaining your answer)
writing_tasks.example: The topic sentence is 'Exercise is essential for good health' because it states the main idea of the paragraph. The off-topic sentence is 'I also like watching movies' because it doesn't relate to exercise or health. This sentence breaks the paragraph's unity and should be removed. All the other sentences support the main idea by explaining specific health benefits of exercise.

grammar_focus.title: Present Simple for General Statements
grammar_focus.explanation: Use present simple in topic sentences to make general statements.
examples: Learning English requires practice. (general statement)
Portland has many parks. (general fact)
Healthy food costs more than junk food. (general truth)
Children need sleep to grow. (general statement)

grammar_focus.title: Transition Words for Supporting Details
grammar_focus.explanation: Use transition words to connect supporting sentences to topic sentence.
examples: First, exercise strengthens muscles. (ordering)
Additionally, it improves mood. (adding information)
For example, walking burns calories. (giving example)
Furthermore, it reduces stress. (adding more support)

grammar_focus.title: Modal Verbs for Recommendations in Topic Sentences
grammar_focus.explanation: Use should/must/can in topic sentences to give recommendations or state possibilities.
examples: Students should study every day. (recommendation)
Everyone must pay taxes. (obligation)
Learning English can improve career options. (possibility)
People should exercise regularly. (advice)

questions.question: What two parts does a topic sentence need?
What is unity in a paragraph?
Where do most paragraphs put the topic sentence?
Every sentence in a paragraph should support the topic sentence.
You can have multiple main ideas in one paragraph.
___, it improves your mood. (transition for adding info)
In the paragraph about Portland food, which sentence was off-topic?

vocabulary.definition: sentence stating main idea of paragraph

vocabulary.example: The main idea is about health.

vocabulary.definition: group of sentences about one idea
vocabulary.example: Write a paragraph about your hobby.

vocabulary.definition: all parts relating to one main idea

vocabulary.example: Stay focused on your main idea.

cultural_notes: American academic writing strongly emphasizes clear topic sentences - teachers look for them in student essays.
In business writing, putting main ideas first (topic sentence at beginning) is called 'front-loading' and is highly valued.
The 'hamburger paragraph' model is commonly taught in U.S. schools: topic sentence (top bun), supporting details (meat), concluding sentence (bottom bun).
American readers expect paragraphs to have clear focus - wandering off-topic is seen as poor organization.
Many American style guides recommend paragraphs of 3-8 sentences for readability.
The five-paragraph essay format (intro paragraph, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, conclusion) is standard in U.S. schools.
